comparator.name: Regenerative Medicine and Technology (BSc)
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 regulations set a 150 EC major and a 30 EC minor. The first two years combine courses with continuing work in laboratory skills, design and academic development. The example uses the 7 EC clinical design project. Year 3 has a 30 EC minor and a 30 EC graduation project combining an internship, an individual thesis and an oral defence. The previous year’s course guide provides context for the named courses retained in the current regulations.

components.name: The Molecular Basis of Life (RMT1001)
components.note: Compulsory; year 1, period 1; chemistry and cell biology in a regenerative-medicine context

components.name: Foundations of Engineering (RMT1002)
components.note: Compulsory; year 1, period 2; mathematics, physics, mechanics of materials, rheology, thermodynamics, circuits, CAD and finite-element modelling

components.name: Regenerative Medicine in Society (RMT1003)
components.note: Compulsory; year 1, period 3; scope, history, ethics and applications of regenerative medicine

components.name: Principles of Medicine (RMT1004)
components.note: Compulsory; year 1, period 4; anatomy, physiology and immunology

components.name: Coding and Data Crunching (RMT1005)
components.note: Compulsory; year 1, period 5; scripting in R, statistics and data analysis

components.name: The Intrinsic Regenerative Capacity of the Human Body (RMT1006)
components.note: Compulsory; year 1, period 6; wound healing, regeneration versus repair, ageing and the limits of regeneration

components.name: Academic Development Line Year 1 (RMT1101)
components.note: Compulsory longitudinal line; learning skills, professional behaviour, scientific storytelling and personal development

components.name: Lab Skills Line Year 1 (RMT1102)
components.note: Compulsory longitudinal line; laboratory skills aligned with the first-year courses

components.name: Attendance Lab Skills Line Year 1 (RMT1112)
components.note: Compulsory; attendance component of the year-1 lab skills line

components.name: Orientation Design Project (RMT1103)
components.note: Compulsory longitudinal line; expert interviews, site visits, journal clubs and a project pitch

components.name: Cells: From Lab to Production (RMT2001)
components.note: Compulsory; year 2, period 1; stem-cell sources, potency, cell manufacture and cell-biomaterial constructs

components.name: Materials Science in Biological Applications (RMT2002)
components.note: Compulsory; year 2, period 2; design, synthesis and characterisation of biomaterials and cell-material interaction

components.name: Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine (RMT2003)
components.note: Compulsory; year 2, period 3; cell therapy, immunotherapy, gene therapy, biomaterials, implants and medical devices

components.name: Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems (RMT2004)
components.note: Compulsory; year 2, period 4; multivariable calculus, differential-equation and data-driven modelling, introduction to neural networks

components.name: Advanced Technologies for Regeneration (RMT2005)
components.note: Compulsory; year 2, period 5; micro- and nanofabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips and biofabrication

components.name: From Research to Market Value (RMT2006)
components.note: Both explore how ideas become marketable products. Maastricht focuses on the value of regenerative-medicine research. UCR teaches general venture design and validation.

components.name: Academic Development Line Year 2 (RMT2101)
components.note: Compulsory longitudinal line; includes choosing electives, minor and thesis subject

components.name: Lab Skills Line Year 2 (RMT2102)
components.note: Compulsory longitudinal line; laboratory skills aligned with the second-year courses

components.name: Attendance Lab Skills Line Year 2 (RMT2112)
components.note: Compulsory; attendance component of the year-2 lab skills line

components.name: Design Project: Clinical Track (RMT2103)
components.note: Selected track of the year-2 design project line (the alternative is the Technological Track, RMT2104, 7 EC)

components.name: Minor (open choice)
components.note: Students complete a 30 EC minor. Choices can include courses at Maastricht or another university, with approval where required.

components.name: Bachelor thesis with internship and presentation/defence (RMT3010, RMT3011, RMT3012)
components.note: Maastricht’s 30 EC graduation project combines an internship, an individual thesis and an oral defence. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled plan.

coreField.label: Biological and molecular foundations of regenerative medicine: biochemistry and the chemistry of life, cell biology, tissue structure and function, stem-cell potency and cell-matrix interaction (The Molecular Basis of Life; Cells: From Lab to Production)

Medical foundations: anatomy, physiology and immunology of the organ systems targeted by regenerative medicine, inflammation, foreign-body response and transplant immunology, wound healing and vascularisation (Principles of Medicine; Technological Trends in Regenerative Medicine)

Engineering, physics and mathematics foundations: vectors, differential equations, mechanics of materials, rheology, thermodynamics, circuits, and the chemistry and materials science needed to design biomedical materials (Foundations of Engineering; Materials Science in Biological Applications)

Advanced regeneration technologies: biomaterials, tissue engineering, micro- and nanofabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips and biofabrication (Materials Science in Biological Applications; Advanced Technologies for Regeneration)

Programming, statistics, data analysis and computational modelling: scripting, probability, regression, data-driven and differential-equation modelling and an introduction to neural networks (Coding and Data Crunching; Data Analysis & Modelling of Biosystems)
Laboratory skills and biomedical laboratory research: lab skills lines in years 1 and 2, experimental design, statistics for experimental data and reporting

Design, innovation and entrepreneurship: the design project lines (analysing a clinical problem, designing and marketing a new application), valorisation and market value, and the ethics of regenerative medicine applications
Academic development: self-regulated learning, professional behaviour, scientific storytelling, personal development and ethical and scientific-integrity standards (Academic Development Lines)
Research training and thesis: a 20-week individual graduation project with thesis and oral defence, preceded by a 30-EC minor

adjacentDirections.label: Biomedical engineering and medical devices: engineering combined with medicine for devices and implants, with medical-device developer as a named career and biomedical engineering and imaging engineering as named further study

progressionAssessment.rationale: Foundations of Life Science precedes cell biology, lab work and anatomy. Cell biology and physiology precede molecular pathology and organ-system disease. Programming, mathematical methods and introductory data analysis precede machine learning. Sustainability Essentials I precedes Sustainability Essentials II. Entrepreneurship precedes market research. Consumer Product Design uses the planned final spring term.

alternativeSelection.assessment: One plan combines biomedical science, laboratory work, engineering foundations and healthcare innovation context. A second device-focused plan could use robotics, signal processing, numerical modelling and physiology, with materials and prototyping. These courses add sensing, control and mechanical modelling, but the catalogue offers limited dedicated study of device design, biomechanics and clinical testing. The material and fabrication direction has complementary chemistry, polymer properties, spectroscopy and sustainable materials design, and cell biology includes stem cells. There is insufficient dedicated work in cell–material interaction, tissue scaffolds, cell manufacture or biofabrication to sustain that direction separately.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both study the molecular basis of life. UCR focuses on proteins, metabolism and biochemical techniques. Maastricht also uses chemistry and cell biology to introduce regenerative medicine.
Both develop cell biology, including cell fate and stem cells. Maastricht extends this to cell sourcing, manufacture and cell–material constructs.
Both develop molecular laboratory skills. Maastricht also integrates lab practice across its first-year courses.
Maastricht awards 2 EC for meeting the first-year laboratory attendance requirement.
Maastricht continues lab training in cell culture, assays and materials. UCR develops related laboratory foundations in its life science lab.
Maastricht awards 2 EC for meeting the second-year laboratory attendance requirement.
Both study organ function and physiology. Maastricht combines physiology with anatomy and immunology in the same course.
Both examine immune responses relevant to regenerative treatments. Maastricht also studies therapies and devices, including implants and cell-based treatments.
Both study tissue repair and regeneration. Maastricht concentrates on the regenerative capacity of different tissues and the factors that limit it.
Maastricht introduces regenerative medicine and its applications in society. UCR covers related biology and general ethics across separate courses.
Both develop quantitative and physical foundations. UCR includes mechanics and material properties in sustainability contexts. Maastricht also teaches engineering tools for biomechanics.
UCR studies material properties and characterisation in sustainability. Maastricht focuses on biomaterials and their interaction with cells.
Maastricht teaches specialist methods such as microfabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips and biofabrication.
Both use programming to explore and analyse data. Maastricht’s course combines R scripting and statistics in regenerative-medicine examples.
Both develop data-driven models. Maastricht combines these with differential equations and examples from biological systems.
Both develop and test product concepts in teams. Maastricht uses a clinical regeneration problem. UCR uses consumer products.
Both explore how ideas become marketable products. Maastricht focuses on the value of regenerative-medicine research. UCR teaches general venture design and validation.
Maastricht introduces the design process through interviews, journal clubs, visits and a project pitch.
Both develop academic, communication and reflective skills. Maastricht continues its academic development sequence throughout the year.
Maastricht continues its academic development sequence and prepares students for their minor and graduation project.
Students complete a 30 EC minor. Choices can include courses at Maastricht or another university, with approval where required.
Maastricht’s 30 EC graduation project combines an internship, an individual thesis and an oral defence. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled plan.

notes.text: Both plans study biochemistry, cell biology, physiology and data analysis. Maastricht adds specialist work in cell manufacture, biomaterials, gene and cell therapies, microfabrication and clinical design. UCR combines biomedical science with related engineering foundations and product design.

Maastricht combines courses with continuing lab, design and academic development work. In the final year, students take a 30 EC minor and complete a 30 EC graduation project. UCR’s optional independent research is separate from the scheduled courses.

audience.programmeDescription: Maastricht’s Regenerative Medicine and Technology bachelor combines biology, medicine and engineering to study ways to repair or regenerate tissues.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The 2026–2027 example uses Maastricht’s clinical design project. The UCR plan combines biomedical science with data analysis, engineering foundations and innovation.

cellNotes.text: Both study the molecular basis of life. UCR focuses on proteins, metabolism and biochemical techniques. Maastricht also uses chemistry and cell biology to introduce regenerative medicine.
Both develop cell biology, including cell fate and stem cells. Maastricht extends this to cell sourcing, manufacture and cell–material constructs.
Both develop molecular laboratory skills. Maastricht also integrates lab practice across its first-year courses.
Maastricht awards 2 EC for meeting the first-year laboratory attendance requirement.
Maastricht continues lab training in cell culture, assays and materials. UCR develops related laboratory foundations in its life science lab.
Maastricht awards 2 EC for meeting the second-year laboratory attendance requirement.
Both study organ function and physiology. Maastricht combines physiology with anatomy and immunology in the same course.
Both examine immune responses relevant to regenerative treatments. Maastricht also studies therapies and devices, including implants and cell-based treatments.
Both study tissue repair and regeneration. Maastricht concentrates on the regenerative capacity of different tissues and the factors that limit it.
Maastricht introduces regenerative medicine and its applications in society. UCR covers related biology and general ethics across separate courses.
Both develop quantitative and physical foundations. UCR includes mechanics and material properties in sustainability contexts. Maastricht also teaches engineering tools for biomechanics.
UCR studies material properties and characterisation in sustainability. Maastricht focuses on biomaterials and their interaction with cells.
Maastricht teaches specialist methods such as microfabrication, microfluidics, organs-on-chips and biofabrication.
Both use programming to explore and analyse data. Maastricht’s course combines R scripting and statistics in regenerative-medicine examples.
Both develop data-driven models. Maastricht combines these with differential equations and examples from biological systems.
Both develop and test product concepts in teams. Maastricht uses a clinical regeneration problem. UCR uses consumer products.
Both explore how ideas become marketable products. Maastricht focuses on the value of regenerative-medicine research. UCR teaches general venture design and validation.
Maastricht introduces the design process through interviews, journal clubs, visits and a project pitch.
Both develop academic, communication and reflective skills. Maastricht continues its academic development sequence throughout the year.
Maastricht continues its academic development sequence and prepares students for their minor and graduation project.
Students complete a 30 EC minor. Choices can include courses at Maastricht or another university, with approval where required.
Maastricht’s 30 EC graduation project combines an internship, an individual thesis and an oral defence. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled plan.
